question: When does an attention model's learned focus identify the input segment that truly determines a label, how can that property be measured objectively, and do sparsity-promoting attention mechanisms improve it?

key_findings.claim: A COCO captioning case study finds that learned attention overlaps annotated objects more than a random sparse map, but the experiment is only a coarse plausibility check.
key_findings.evidence: For generated words manually associated with COCO object classes, cosine overlap between upsampled attention and the relevant bounding-box mask averages 0.539, versus 0.24 for a random 20-location vector and 0.429 after retaining the learned map's top 20 locations. The annotation-to-word mapping, bounding-box proxy, and single captioning architecture do not establish causal faithfulness.

key_findings.claim: Selective Dependence Classification (SDC) and the Focus-Classify Attention Model (FCAM) make one narrow notion of attention interpretability objectively measurable.
key_findings.evidence: An SDC example contains one foreground segment drawn from the label-conditional distribution and independently drawn background segments. FCAM scores segments, softmax-aggregates them, and classifies the aggregate; Focus Truth (FT) is the probability that the true foreground scores above every background segment. The paper explicitly acknowledges that one-segment dependence and conditional independence are cartoon-like assumptions.

key_findings.claim: High classification accuracy does not identify the intended foreground, even when an interpretable solution exists.
key_findings.evidence: Three two-dimensional constructions reach 100% classification accuracy with only about 67-70% FT: optimization can settle on a focus rule that treats one class as background; the focus hypothesis class can be unable to separate foreground from background; or a powerful classifier can decode an almost uniformly averaged input before useful focusing is learned. These are constructive synthetic failure modes, not an exhaustive theorem for modern Transformer attention.

anchors.section: Section 4.3, third error mode and training dynamics

key_findings.claim: On semi-synthetic CIFAR-SDC, sparsemax and spherical softmax improve foreground selection without a material accuracy gain.
key_findings.evidence: With input-level aggregation, vanilla softmax obtains 95.04% accuracy and 79.77% FT; sparsemax obtains 95.80% and 91.43%, and spherical softmax 95.17% and 91.07%. Entropy regularization remains at 79.97% FT, while hard attention reaches 87.63% FT but lowers accuracy to 92.13%. Results are averaged over three runs except some entropy configurations use fewer runs.

anchors.section: Appendix D.0.1, seed and hyperparameter protocol

key_findings.claim: The full results contradict any blanket claim that sparsity itself makes attention interpretable.
key_findings.evidence: On the fully synthetic SDC task, input-level sparsemax has slightly lower FT than softmax (77.076% versus 77.80%), spherical softmax falls to 71.83%, and hard attention collapses to 12.07% FT despite 97.264% accuracy. Later-layer aggregation, rather than sparsity alone, raises several FT values into the high 80s. The defensible conclusion is algorithm- and representation-dependent improvement, not a general sparsity guarantee.

method.core_idea: Replace the ambiguous claim that attention is interpretable with a controlled classification problem whose label-relevant segment is known to the evaluator but hidden during training.
method.mechanism: Generate mosaics with one foreground segment, train a focus network and classifier end to end from class labels, compare the focus network's top-ranked segment with the latent foreground index, and test softmax, entropy regularization, sparsemax, spherical softmax, hard attention, and different aggregation layers.
assumptions: Exactly one segment determines the complete class label.
Foreground and background segments are conditionally independent and drawn from distinct base distributions.
Ranking the foreground first is a sufficient operational definition of interpretability for this task.
Semi-synthetic mosaic behavior is informative about attention failures in natural structured data.
The optimization and architecture comparisons are not dominated by unreported hyperparameter or seed effects.

techniques.role: Creates a task with evaluator-known latent relevance and label-only training supervision.
Separates segment scoring, weighted aggregation, and downstream classification.
Measures whether the true foreground segment receives the largest focus score.
Tests entropy regularization, sparsemax, spherical softmax, and hard selection as possible interpretability interventions.
Tests whether aggregating learned hidden features rather than raw segments improves focusing.

evaluations.setting: Show-Attend-and-Tell-style image captioning on COCO object words with bounding-box metadata.
evaluations.metric: Cosine overlap between an upsampled attention map and the corresponding object mask.
evaluations.result: Learned attention averages 0.539 overlap, above a random-20 baseline at 0.24 and a binarized top-20 learned map at 0.429.
evaluations.baseline: Random sparse locations and the learned attention map reduced to its top 20 locations.

evaluations.setting: Three controlled two-dimensional SDC constructions with 200 training mosaics and nine segments per mosaic.
evaluations.result: Training produces fully accurate FCAMs with roughly one-third of examples focused incorrectly under three distinct mechanisms.
evaluations.baseline: Existence of simple accurate-and-interpretable focus/classifier solutions where the construction permits them.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-SDC with 40,000 mosaics, 10,000 test mosaics, three foreground classes, seven background classes, and CNN focus/classifier modules.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, FT, attention nonzero count, distance to a coordinate vector, and entropy.
evaluations.result: Sparsemax and spherical softmax improve FT by more than ten points at similar accuracy; entropy regularization does not, and hard attention pays an accuracy cost.
evaluations.baseline: Vanilla softmax FCAM at raw-input and sixth-layer aggregation.

evaluations.setting: Low-dimensional synthetic SDC with five seeds and input- versus hidden-layer aggregation.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, FT, and three sparsity measures.
evaluations.result: No input-level sparse variant beats vanilla softmax FT, hard attention fails sharply, and hidden-layer aggregation is the more consistent improvement.
evaluations.baseline: Vanilla softmax under the same aggregation layer.

limitations: SDC assumes one fully label-determining foreground segment and independent background segments, unlike most natural vision and language tasks.
FT measures localization against a generative index; it does not test counterfactual causal necessity, sufficiency, stability, or usefulness to a human.
FCAM is much simpler than multi-head self-attention with residual streams, value vectors, and information mixed across layers.
CIFAR-SDC is semi-synthetic: foreground and background are separated by class identity and every mosaic uses exactly nine complete images.
The COCO evaluation relies on manually grouped output words and rectangular object masks that may not represent the evidence actually required to generate a caption.
The CIFAR comparisons use only three runs, some entropy entries use two runs, and no uncertainty intervals are reported.
Hyperparameter selection is described only coarsely, and the many mechanism/layer combinations invite selection effects.
The study does not evaluate modern pretrained Transformers, cross-attention, long-context behavior, or real user judgments of explanations.
failure_modes: The classifier learns to decode an average of all segments, leaving the focus module untrained or misleading.
The focus function treats a legitimate foreground class as if it were background while the classifier compensates.
The focus hypothesis class cannot represent the foreground/background boundary, so two wrong modules compose into an accurate predictor.
A sparse distribution confidently selects the wrong segment, increasing apparent decisiveness without faithfulness.
Contextual encoders move information between positions before attention, breaking the correspondence between a high weight and the original input segment.
An evaluator mistakes localization plausibility for a causal explanation of the complete model.
reusable_insights: Evaluate predictive accuracy and explanation alignment separately; one cannot substitute for the other.
Use controlled latent-relevance tasks as unit tests before making interpretability claims on natural data.
Report counterexamples and per-mechanism results rather than compressing all sparsity interventions into one conclusion.
A good faithfulness benchmark should vary focus capacity, classifier capacity, aggregation depth, and data ambiguity independently.
Ground-truth localization is useful but should be paired with interventions that test whether selected information is necessary and sufficient.
open_questions: Can SDC be generalized to multiple interacting foreground segments, structured rationales, and context-dependent relevance without losing objective evaluation?
Which training objectives make attention both causally faithful and calibrated rather than merely sparse?
How do residual connections and value-vector mixing change the three FCAM failure modes in Transformers?
Can a model know when its attention explanation is unreliable on an individual example?
Do attention explanations that score well under FT improve human decisions, debugging, or error discovery?
What benchmark combines latent ground truth, counterfactual interventions, naturalistic inputs, and human-usefulness tests?

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not Explanation
competitive_landscape.difference: Jain and Wallace test correlations with gradient importance and construct alternative attention distributions on natural-language classifiers; the reviewed paper instead creates evaluator-known foreground labels and directly scores localization in a controlled FCAM.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not not Explanation
competitive_landscape.difference: Wiegreffe and Pinter argue that explanation must be defined model-relatively and propose seed-calibrated, uniform, diagnostic, and end-to-end adversarial tests; SDC supplies objective relevance labels but only under a far narrower data-generating process.

competitive_landscape.title: Is Attention Interpretable?
competitive_landscape.difference: Serrano and Smith erase or manipulate intermediate representations to measure attention weights' effect on predictions; the reviewed work compares attention to a known foreground index, which is clearer but does not itself measure causal effect.

competitive_landscape.title: How (Un)Faithful is Attention?
competitive_landscape.difference: Amini and Kosseim derive AtteFa from one-shot adversarial attention and test contextual versus non-contextual encoders in text classification; FT instead requires ground-truth segment identity and tests whether the top focus is correct.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Faithfulness of Vision Transformer Explanations
competitive_landscape.difference: Wu et al. evaluate saliency faithfulness for Vision Transformer explanations with grouped perturbations and find gradient/multi-layer aggregation useful; this addresses modern attention stacks absent from the FCAM study, but lacks SDC's exact latent foreground variable.

novelty_assessment: The paper's strongest contribution is not a universal verdict on attention but a clean, testable micro-world in which relevance is hidden from training and known to evaluation, enabling exact examples of accurate-but-misfocused models. The three failure constructions and layer/mechanism ablations are useful. Novelty should be scoped tightly: FT is one localization criterion under unrealistic SDC assumptions, the COCO study is plausibility rather than causal evidence, and the appendix contradicts a general claim that sparse attention is more interpretable.
reviewer_notes: Read all 24 cached pages, including the COCO protocol, SDC/FCAM definitions, all three error-mode constructions, both main and appendix result tables, seed/hyperparameter notes, manual object-word mappings, and references. Five direct primary-source competitors were checked on 2026-08-23. Scope audit: claims apply to one-segment SDC/FCAM localization, not attention interpretability in general. Contradiction audit: the synthetic appendix shows sparsemax, spherical softmax, and especially hard attention can fail to improve FT, so the main-text sparsity conclusion must remain conditional.
